articles.title: Who was Madhav Mantri? The Mumbai cricket stalwart with four Tests who helped shape Sunil Gavaskar and stood alongside teenage Sachin Tendulkar in 1990
articles.summary: Cricket News: When the Mumbai Cricket Association decided to name lounges at the Wankhede Stadium after Sachin Tendulkar, Ajinkya Rahane and late Madhav Mantri, the.
articles.body: When the Mumbai Cricket Association decided to name lounges at the Wankhede Stadium after Sachin Tendulkar, Ajinkya Rahane and late Madhav Mantri, the first two names needed little explanation. The third may leave younger cricket fans wondering: who was Madhav Mantri?The answer is a story of influence far greater than his four-Test career suggests.Mantri was a three-time Ranji Trophy-winning captain of Bombay, a national selector and a prominent administrator who played a role in shaping Mumbai cricket's culture. He also had a remarkable connection with two of India's greatest batters, Sunil Gavaskar and Tendulkar, at very different stages of their careers.The man who taught Gavaskar to earn his India capMantri was Gavaskar's maternal uncle, and his influence on the future India great began well before Gavaskar's international debut.As a youngster, Gavaskar was fascinated by an India cap belonging to Mantri. He wanted to have it, but his uncle refused to let him simply inherit it. Gavaskar would have to earn his own.When Gavaskar eventually received an India cap during India's 1971 tour of the West Indies, he did not wear it in the tour matches. He waited until he had actually represented India in a Test.For Mantri, the cap represented something that had to be earned.His own international career was brief. He made his Test debut against England in 1951 and played his last international against Pakistan in 1955. Across four Tests, he scored 67 runs, with a highest score of 39.But those numbers barely tell the story of his standing in Indian domestic cricket.Three Ranji Trophy titles with BombayMantri played 42 Ranji Trophy matches for Bombay and accumulated 2,787 runs at an average of 50.67. His finest innings came against Maharashtra in the 1948-49 season, when he scored 200 in a match that produced 2,376 runs and nine centuries.His greater legacy came as a leader.Mantri captained Bombay to Ranji Trophy titles in 1951-52, 1955-56 and 1956-57, helping establish the foundations of the dominance that would later become synonymous with Mumbai cricket.There was also an unfortunate slice of Test history attached to his career. During the 1952 Headingley Test against England, India were reduced to 0/4 in their second innings, with Fred Trueman and Alec Bedser ripping through the batting order. Mantri was one of those four batters dismissed before India had scored a run.His international career faded. His influence on Mumbai cricket did not.The batting lesson behind Gavaskar's greatnessMantri's impact on Gavaskar went beyond the famous India-cap story.On one occasion, Gavaskar returned home delighted after scoring around 290 in a college match during a huge partnership. But Mantri was less interested in the number. His immediate question was how Gavaskar had been dismissed.Gavaskar explained that he had fallen attempting a lofted shot while his partner remained unbeaten.Mantri's response was straightforward: do not give your wicket away. Make the bowler earn it.That philosophy would become central to Gavaskar's batting. The opener went on to score 10,122 Test runs and became the first batter to cross 10,000 in the format.Mantri's Test tally was only 67.Yet one of the defining principles behind India's first great batting superstar had been reinforced by a man whose own international career lasted just four Tests.From Gavaskar to a teenage TendulkarMantri's influence did not stop with his nephew.He later served as a national selector and played a role in backing Ajit Wadekar's selection for India. He also became president of the Mumbai Cricket Association and treasurer of the BCCI.Then, nearly four decades after his own Test debut, Mantri found himself alongside another teenage Mumbai batting prodigy.He was India's team manager on the 1990 tour of England, when a 17-year-old Tendulkar was beginning to establish himself at international level.At Old Trafford, with India battling to save the second Test, Tendulkar struck an unbeaten 119, his maiden Test century. He became India's youngest Test centurion at the time.Mantri was there as team manager as another Mumbai batter announced himself on the world stage.The teenager's hunger also impressed him. Tendulkar was expected to be rested for a match against Derbyshire but wanted to play because he wanted to face Ian Bishop, one of the fastest bowlers around. He got his chance and scored an unbeaten century.After Tendulkar's Old Trafford hundred, Mantri recalled that the teenager was not simply interested in celebrating. He wanted to know whether he had made mistakes during his innings.For Mantri, who had spent decades emphasising discipline and responsibility, that attitude mattered.Why Madhav Mantri still mattersThat is the real story behind the name now being attached to a lounge at Wankhede.Mantri may have scored only 67 Test runs, but his cricketing footprint was considerably larger. He led Bombay to three Ranji Trophy titles, influenced selection, held senior administrative positions and helped shape the thinking of Gavaskar.Decades later, he was also part of the Indian team setup when Tendulkar scored the first of his 100 international centuries.One Mumbai cricket generation followed another, and Mantri was there in the background for both.The MCA's decision to name a Wankhede lounge after him alongside Tendulkar and Rahane brings that forgotten legacy back into focus.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Heads Dada wins, tails Ponting loses: When Sourav Ganguly pranked Australian captain at toss with 'head-tail' call
articles.summary: Cricket News: Sourav Ganguly is widely regarded as one of the most influential captains in Indian cricket history. During his career, \"Dada\" was known for several m.
articles.body: Sourav Ganguly is widely regarded as one of the most influential captains in Indian cricket history. During his career, "Dada" was known for several memorable moments on and off the field, from making Steve Waugh wait at the toss and celebrating shirtless on the Lord's balcony to clashes with coaches Greg Chappell and John Buchanan, arguments with Shane Warne, and refusing to walk after Graeme Smith claimed a catch.But former Australia captain Michael Clarke has shared another story that shows a lighter side of Ganguly.In his book Eleven Gods and a Billion Indians, author Boria Majumdar quotes Clarke recalling an incident involving Ganguly and Ricky Ponting during a toss in India, although Clarke admits he does not remember which match it was.“One of Clarke’s favourite anecdotes goes thus: Ganguly and Ricky Ponting were out at the toss during one of the matches in India — Clarke doesn’t specifically remember which one — and Ponting had the coin in hand. Just as he flipped the coin, Ganguly, if Clarke is to be believed, said, ‘Head-Tail’.“‘Trust me, mate, that’s what Ricky told me,’ Clarke says, cracking up. ‘Ricky said he couldn’t fathom what had happened with Dada having said Head-Tail. [And, apparently it was said at the speed of lightning.] It had taken Ricky a second or two to come to grips with the situation and by that time the coin had come down. Ganguly just picked it up and said to Ricky, “We’ll bat” and walked off. India had won the toss and were batting. Ricky did not really know what to do or say and all he did was tell us in the dressing room exactly what happened at the toss," Clarke was quoted as saying in the book.Clarke is not sure which match the incident took place in.According to available records, Ganguly won five tosses against Ricky Ponting, and all of those came outside India; twice during the 2003 World Cup and three times in the 2003-04 VB Series. That means Clarke may have mixed up the venue while recalling the story, as Ponting would have been the one calling the toss if the match had been played in India.Clarke, however, clearly states that he does not remember the exact match in which the incident happened.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: England clinch Test series sweep of Pakistan: Joe Root and Jordan Cox steer hosts to eight-wicket win at Edgbaston
articles.summary: England secure first home series whitewash of Pakistan with eight-wicket victory in third Test at Edgbaston after Mohammad Abbas opened day four with wickets of Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay in first over; Joe Root - bowled off a no-ball - and Jordan Cox notch unbeaten fifties in win
articles.body:
The thought of England losing the Test match would have been unthinkable when Ollie Robinson reduced the visitors to 0-2 on the second evening - Pakistan still trailing by 320 at the time - but it looked a genuine possibility when the hosts themselves lost two in their first over to start the fourth morning.

Ben Duckett (0) signed off a miserable series by nicking off first ball to Mohammad Abbas (2-27), who added Emilio Gay (0) lbw to finish a stunning opener.

But any fears of England succumbing to a calamitous defeat were soon dispelled by their skipper as Joe Root (62no) struck a fine fifty, sharing an unbroken 128-run partnership with Jordan Cox (59no), who notched his third half-century late on, to secure victory in 24.2 overs.

Pakistan, meanwhile, will be left wondering would could have been, had Mohammad Ali not overstepped when bowling Root for 23 - dragging onto his stumps off a no-ball - with England just 35-2 at the time.

Will England stick with Cox for South Africa?

Cox's knock will have aided his hopes of retaining a spot in England's starting XI when the Test team are next in action for the three-match tour of South Africa, starting on December 17.

Jacob Bethell - injured for the Pakistan series - is expected to return to the side, but could he or Cox open the batting instead of Gay?

And were Gay to retain his place at the top of the order, Cox could yet fill in at wicketkeeper instead of Jamie Smith, who didn't keep during Pakistan's second innings due to an injured finger - though he has three months for that to sufficiently heal.

Pakistan were briefly hopeful of successfully defending a total of 130 or less in a Test match for the first time since 1993, when New Zealand were bowled out for 93, chasing 127, at Hamilton.

The last such instance of 130 or less being defended in England was when England set Australia 124 in the 1997 Ashes at The Oval and bowled them out for 104.

Pakistan unearth gem in Razaullah after series of struggles

In what has otherwise been a dismal series for Pakistan, they at least leave having shown some fight in this final Test by taking things into a fourth day and setting a target that briefly troubled England.

Also, in 21-year-old Razaullah, they have certainly unearthed a raw gem. The debutant knocked over England's all-time leading run-scorer Root in the first innings with just his fourth ball in Test cricket, on his way to a four-wicket haul, while his exploits with the bat on the third evening will live long in the memory.

When Pakistan's eighth second-innings wicket fell, they still trailed by two runs - England looking set to clinch their series sweep inside three days - before Razaullah proceeded to smash 81 off only 63 balls, clearing the ropes a staggering nine times to equal Tim Southee's record for a debutant.

Ultimately though, England are well deserving of the 3-0 series scoreline to herald Root's return as Test captain following Ben Stokes' international retirement earlier in the summer.

Root pleased with how England have dealt with 'chaos'

"The amount of uncertainty, noise and I guess chaos there was coming into the series, the way the guys have dealt with that - being so clinical with what we've had in front of us - and be stood here with a 3-0 win is really pleasing.

"We were clinical towards the back end there, a big partnership to see us home. It's exactly the sort of thing we're after and puts us in a nice place going into the winter.

"From 2-2, to be able to see that home with two guys set at the end, is a step forward in the right direction.

"The fact that everyone is contrubuting shows that they're good enough to perform at this level, which is a really good thing.

"We'll have different challenges in the winter and different surfaces, but can we keep taking strides forward as a group? Guys going on and making big contributions [hundred] will be one of them. That being said, we still made 400 twice in these testing conditions."

Butch: A lot of good things about England

"They were made to sweat for it at times, which is a good thing.

"It gave England pause for thought at times when it comes to differing conditions in Test matches - particularly with regards to South Africa and the ball not moving laterally as much.

"Perhaps a slight concern about the lack of centuries by the batters, but there was a lot of good things about England this Test match series.

"They weren't given much of a challenge for most of it, which is why yesterday was such a pleasing day as far as the summer is concerned."

Urooj: Major problems for Pakistan cricket

"There are problems with Pakistan cricket, major problems. They lost this series, drew in the West Indies, lost to Bangladesh at home, where their record isn't particularly good.

"They have now lost 11 out of 12 away from home and 15 out of the last 20 Test matches. Those are telling figures, as were the size of England's wins.

"Pakistan maybe had just one good day of cricket in the Test series. There are ingredients to work with but a lot needs to be done right for longer periods of time if there is to be a brighter Pakistan future."

First Test (Headingley) - England won by innings and 103 runs

Second Test (Lord's) - England won by 194 runs

Third Test (Edgbaston) - England won by eight wickets

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Joe Root and Jordan Cox come through scare to win third Test and 3-0 sweep
articles.summary: England survive an almighty scare to eventually win the third Test against Pakistan by eight wickets and complete a 3-0 clean sweep.
articles.body:
Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day four of five)

Pakistan 133 (Tongue 4-42) & 449 (Masood 95, Razaullah 81, Babar 76, Awais 59)

England 453 (Brook 75, Smith 69, Lawrence 65, Gay 60, Robinson 50; Razaullah 4-148) & 130-2 (Root 62*, Cox 59*)

England won by eight wickets, won series 3-0

England survived an almighty scare to eventually win the third Test against Pakistan by eight wickets and complete a 3-0 clean sweep.

The home side were already facing an unexpected chase of 130 on the fourth day after being frazzled by the hitting of Pakistan debutant Razaullah on Friday evening.

And the prospect of one of Test cricket's greatest turnarounds was raised when England were reduced to 2-2 in the opening over. Ben Duckett edged Muhammad Abbas' first ball behind and Emilio Gay was palpably leg before.

England could have been 35-3 after Joe Root rashly dragged on to his own stumps off Mohammad Ali. Ali was found to have overstepped and Root was reprieved on 23.

While Root needed fortune, Jordan Cox once again impressed with a composed 59, a further claim for the Essex man to be in the XI for the first Test against South Africa in December.

Cox and Root shared an unbroken stand of 128, Root unbeaten on 62 when victory was sealed just before lunch.

For Root, this completes a successful return to the captaincy he resumed when Ben Stokes retired in June, while England end one of their most turbulent summers in history in a positive fashion.

They switch formats to begin a white-ball series against Sri Lanka in Southampton on Tuesday, with Brendon McCullum back in charge and Kevin Pietersen as part of the coaching staff .

England in better place than start of summer - Root

Who has given selectors food for thought? England-Pakistan player ratings

Hesson open to Pakistan job after England approach

England come through much-needed challenge

Such was England's serene progress up to the third evening of the final Test of the series, it was easy to forget that they were without both a captain and a coach less than two months ago.

For all the good things they have done against Pakistan, there was the feeling their credentials had not been challenged by the dismal performances of the tourists.

When Pakistan were 0-2 in their second innings, England could have won in two days. From then on, the visitors finally found some fight and England were asked to respond. The way Root's side coped with the pressure was not entirely convincing.

Their tactics in the field collapsed in the face of Razaullah's assault on Friday, then their batting was wobbling on Saturday morning. An extra hundred runs on the target might have been difficult. How Pakistan will rue being dismissed for 133 on the first day.

It is to England's credit that they weathered the storm. Even if it took Pakistan two and a half matches to show up, England have still won three consecutive Tests after a previous run of two wins in 10.

Greater challenges await on the winter trips to South Africa, Bangladesh and Australia. New head coach Stephen Fleming arrives in the UK in the coming days with plenty in his in-tray.

One area of concern for Fleming will be England's openers, albeit if the modest returns of Duckett and Gay have come in a summer when ball has been on top of bat.

In a dramatic start to the day, Abbas' metronomic accuracy not only sent nerves through the England dressing room, but also further exposed a growing issue at the top of the order.

Duckett edged a beauty for a golden duck. Although he has registered England's only century of the summer, Duckett has not reached 20 in five innings against Pakistan and his average since the beginning of the Ashes is 23.

Gay has three half-centuries in his first summer as a Test cricketer, though being pinned on the shin by Abbas left his average below 25. Gay swished his bat in the direction of the stumps in frustration and wasted a review, his immediate future in the team vulnerable.

At 2-2, the pressure on England was as high as the tension among the modest Edgbaston crowd. That Cox was able to navigate the hosts to safety has massively boosted his chances of remaining when Jacob Bethell returns from injury, possibly at the expense of Gay.

Cox was more secure than his senior partner, Root. Not only did the captain survive the Ali no-ball, he also edged between the static slips off a furious Abbas when he had 34.

The miss sucked the hope from Pakistan and England were able to accelerate towards their target.

Bar the past 48 hours, this has been a shambolic series from Pakistan, who have been behind since Ollie Robinson trapped Azan Awais lbw from the first ball of the first Test at Headingley.

Pakistan threatened to abandon the second Test over an interview broadcast by Sky with the sons of Imran Khan. After the defeat at Lord's, they replaced head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed with Mike Hesson and dropped seven players from the squad - the ramifications of which look set to continue back at home.

There was a genuine chance of a two-day humiliation in Birmingham, so the Friday fightback was as welcome as it was unexpected. The top order finally found a way to cope with the England attack and Razaullah's pyrotechnics will live long in the memory.

Razaullah was one of the seven players called into the squad. He had already impressed with his pace bowling, dismissing Root in his first over in Test cricket, then the way he dismantled the England attack on Friday was thrilling and audacious.

Pakistan may have found a star in the making, a silver lining to a terrible tour.

articles.title: England complete 3-0 Test series clean sweep with 8-wicket win over Pakistan at Edgbaston
articles.summary: Cricket News: Joe Root led England to a 3-0 Test series whitewash over Pakistan after scoring an unbeaten 62 in the third Test at Edgbaston. England were chasing 13.
articles.body: Joe Root led England to a 3-0 Test series whitewash over Pakistan after scoring an unbeaten 62 in the third Test at Edgbaston. England were chasing 130 for victory but got off to a poor start. Ben Duckett was dismissed by Mohammad Abbas with the first ball of the innings, while opener Emilio Gay also fell later in the same over.At 2 for 2, Pakistan had a chance to put England under pressure. But Root and Jordan Cox remained calm and slowly took control of the chase.It was the first time England had whitewashed Pakistan in a home Test series.Root survived a big scare when Mohammad Ali bowled him for 23, only for the delivery to be called a no-ball. It was Ali’s 17th no-ball of the series.Pakistan then missed another opportunity when Root, on 38, edged Abbas between first and second slip. Neither fielder went for the catch.Root made Pakistan pay for the missed chances. His unbeaten 62 was his 110th Test innings of 50 or more, a tally that includes 41 centuries.Cox remained unbeaten on 59 as England reached the target in the 25th over with eight wickets in hand.Root praises Pakistan's fightPakistan had shown more fight in the third Test after conceding a huge 320-run first-innings deficit.Root said the difficult chase was useful for England after Pakistan had put them under pressure."Fair play to Pakistan, ?they threw some punches last night. They made it very difficult for us and in some ways it's a good thing to go through that," said Root."Test cricket is not always going to go your own way but to see us actually be quite clinical with the bat off the back of that was good too. So ?in many ways we're better for it."Of course there’s things we will want to improve on but we ?came into this ?series with a lot of question marks and a lot of noise around the team and we’ve walked away 3-0 winners so ?in that respect I’m quite ?pleased."England bounce back after difficult periodThe series came after a difficult period for England, who had been looking to recover from their defeat to New Zealand following the Ashes loss.Root's return to the captaincy after Ben Stokes' retirement from international cricket ended with a series whitewash.Pakistan had one major positive in the third Test. Debutant Razaullah scored an impressive 81 off 63 balls, giving his team hope and bringing energy to the contest at Edgbaston.Robinson leads England's pace attackEngland's fast bowlers were once again too strong for Pakistan on helpful surfaces.Ollie Robinson led the attack and finished the series with 21 wickets to be named England's player of the series.“I’m a realist, I know it's not always going to be like this,” said Robinson, England’s player of the series.“We know there’s ?going to be tougher times ahead. We have some tough opposition coming up and we’re looking forward to the challenge."Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson also played important roles in England's dominant series win.England's batting was less convincing, with no batter managing to score a century in the three Tests.Jacob Bethell is expected to return for the winter tour after recovering from knee surgery. That could leave one of Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence or Cox fighting for a place in the team.Cox, who also kept wicket in the second innings because of Jamie Smith’s finger injury, strengthened his case with his unbeaten 59.Pakistan face more questions after 3-0 lossThe defeat was another setback for Pakistan, who have now lost 16 of their last 21 Tests.Their tour was also marked by major changes. Seven players were replaced in the squad after the second Test, while coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul were sacked.Pakistan captain Babar Azam said the team had some positive moments but blamed their first-innings batting for the defeat.“We had a couple of good moments. I think we have bowled well but I think the first innings cost us. Too many soft dismissals,” said Pakistan captain Babar Azam.“I think this was a good opportunity for youngsters to play against quality bowlers, quality opponent, so they learned a lot and I think this is helpful for the future."Pakistan will now turn their attention to their next assignment against Sri Lanka in October.England, meanwhile, will face South Africa in a three-Test series in December and January. Marcus Trescothick, who had taken over as interim red-ball head coach after Brendon McCullum's departure, will hand the team over to Stephen Fleming.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: England vs Pakistan player ratings: Has Jordan Cox given selectors food for thought?
articles.summary: Which batter played his most mature innings of the year? Who has given the selectors food for thought? Player ratings from England's win over Pakistan at Edgbaston.
articles.body:
England have wrapped up victory over Pakistan in the third Test by eight wickets to seal a 3-0 series win.

Here's how the players rated at Edgbaston.

Emilio Gay - 6 - A gritty Test-best of 60 in tricky batting conditions in the first innings looked to have gone some way towards securing his place on the plane for a winter tour of South Africa, only for a duck next time round to bring back some uncertainty. (Series - 6)

Ben Duckett - 2 - A miserable end to the summer for the opener who will now come under some scrutiny. Made 11 and zero in this match and finishes this three-Test series well down the averages with a disappointing 44 runs at 8.8. (Series - 2)

Jordan Cox - 7 - A cheap dismissal in the first innings but made a nerveless unbeaten 59 to take the sting out of Pakistan after a wobble in the chase. A particularly impressive effort with the gloves - taking five dismissals - after being called upon to keep following Jamie Smith's injury may have given the selectors food for thought in the role. (Series - 7)

Joe Root - 7 - Question marks over his captaincy during Pakistan's second innings, but got England over the line with 62 not out. A 10th lbw in 14 innings suggests a technical issue which still needs to be ironed out by England's all-time leading run-scorer. (Series - 7)

Harry Brook - 7 - Batted with real discipline and focus at a time when Pakistan had a foothold in the game on day one. His most mature Test knock this year. Ran himself out on 75 when a century beckoned but forgivable given the application he showed earlier. Finishes as leading run-scorer in the series with 215 runs at 53.75. (Series - 8)

Dan Lawrence - 7 - Having been shunted around the order the Surrey all-rounder batted with the kind of confidence to suggest he might deserve a sustained run in the middle during a measured 65. Bowling underused but a not-too-shabby batting average of 46.75 will help his winter touring prospects. (Series - 7)

Jamie Smith - 6 - Not quite back to his fluent best but will be satisfied to notch up useful half-centuries in consecutive Tests. Kept reasonably well in Pakistan's first innings before a finger injury kept him off the field in the second. (Series - 6)

Gus Atkinson - 6 - Wicketless in the first innings and it initially looked like it was going to be another hard-luck tale. However, he shook off the weariness and a change to the City End allowed him to pocket three wickets to lighten his mood. (Series - 5)

Jofra Archer - 7 - Took a bit of tap in the second innings but bowled with plenty of zip and aggression throughout. A brutal ball to dismiss Saud Shakeel was a reminder of his menace. England will be desperate to keep him fit and firing during a pivotal 12 months. (Series - 8)

Ollie Robinson - 8 - Is there anyone better with a Dukes ball in English conditions? Another masterclass in control. England's tone-setter finishes the series with 21 wickets at a miserly 8.76. A breezy half-century on day two also entertained the crowd. (Series - 9)

Josh Tongue - 7 - Mopped up the tourists' lower order in the first innings with 4-42. Healthy returns in all three Tests - 19 wickets in all - and continues to look a vital cog in the machine. (Series - 8)

England in better place than start of summer - Root

Hesson open to Pakistan job after England approach

Azan Awais - 7 - Still finding his feet at Test level. Made a battling 59 off 84 balls in the second innings, after Pakistan were reduced to 0-2, and looks a player worth persisting with.

Saim Ayub - 1 - Called up for this Test after wholesale changes to the Pakistan side and looked drastically undercooked having not played a first-class fixture since October last year. Almost inevitably he bagged a pair. Scrapes a point for leaving the CPL at the drop of a hat to turn up.

Abdullah Shafique - 1 - Two half-centuries in the series but under leaden skies he was easy meat for Robinson and snared by the Sussex slayer for three and nought.

Shan Masood - 8 - A tame dismissal in the first innings but rolled up his sleeves second time around as he manufactured a composed and defiant 95 to top score for the tourists.

Babar Azam - 6 - Provided a reminder that with bat in hand, on his day, he is up there with the best players in the world to watch. A classy 76 was too little, too late, and as a polarising figure in Pakistan cricket might feel the heat in his role as captain.

Saud Shakeel - 6 - Rode his luck on occasions as he top-scored in the first innings with 43 then made 29 before being on the end of rasping bouncer from Archer. Finished Pakistan's leading run-scorer in the series with 204 at 34.00.

Ghazi Ghori - 2 - A largely unremarkable debut with the bat - scores of four and 16 - and struggled keeping wicket when he had to stand up to the stumps for large periods, leaking 18 byes.

Mohammad Imran - 6 - The most economical of Pakistan's bowlers who brought some vital control to curtail England's free scoring.

Razaullah Khan - 9 - A star is born. The 21-year-old brought a bit of bite to the Pakistan attack and was reminiscent of a young Waqar Younis as he took 4-148 in the first innings. Yet it was a mesmerising innings of 81 with the bat, featuring a joint-best nine sixes, which left an indelible impression.

Mohammad Ali - 5 - Hunted for wickets and beat the bat on a number of occasions but lacked the necessary consistency and control. Needs to iron out his no-ball issue which cost him Root's wicket in the second innings.

Muhammad Abbas - 7 - Pakistan's 'Mr Dependable' kept stoically plugging away as he shouldered much of the bowling burden for the tourists at the age of 36. Made useful lower-order runs to help force England to bat again, then got the ball talking on day four to give the hosts a fright.

articles.title: 138 years later, England-Pakistan series creates rare Test cricket feat
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: England completed a 3-0 Test series clean sweep over Pakistan at Edgbaston, but the series produced an unusual statistic.It was only the ei.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: England completed a 3-0 Test series clean sweep over Pakistan at Edgbaston, but the series produced an unusual statistic.It was only the eighth three-match Test series in history to finish without a single individual century. It was also only the second such series in England, after the 1888 Ashes.England's batting was led by Joe Root, who remained unbeaten on 62 in the third Test, while Jordan Cox scored an unbeaten 59 as England chased down 130 with eight wickets in hand.The result gave England their second 3-0 Test series clean sweep over Pakistan, after their success in the 2022/23 series. It was also England's 15th three-match Test series sweep overall.For Pakistan, it was their 11th Test series defeat by a 3-0 margin.Root survives early scare to finish the jobEngland's chase got off to a shocking start when Ben Duckett was dismissed for a duck with the first ball. Emilio Gay then fell later in the same over bowled by Mohammad Abbas.At 2 for 2, Pakistan had a chance to put England under serious pressure.But Root settled things down. He survived a major scare when Mohammad Ali bowled him for 23, only for the delivery to be called a no-ball.It was Ali's 17th no-ball of the series.Root had another lucky escape when, on 38, he edged Abbas between first and second slip. Neither fielder went for the catch.The England batter made Pakistan pay for the missed opportunities. He went on to complete his 110th score of 50 or more in Test cricket, including 41 centuries.Cox gives Root strong supportJordan Cox provided excellent support for Root as the pair took control of the chase.Cox remained unbeaten on 59 and helped England reach the target in just 25 overs.Pakistan had shown plenty of fight in the third Test after conceding a massive 320-run first-innings lead. But England's dominance in the first two Tests meant the series was already heavily tilted in their favour.Had Pakistan shown the same fight earlier in the series, the contest could have been much closer.England's bowlers make the differenceEngland's fast bowlers were the biggest difference between the two sides.Ollie Robinson led the attack and finished the series with 21 wickets. Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson also played important roles as England's pace attack made the most of helpful conditions.The batting, however, was less convincing.No England batter scored a century across the three Tests, making the series only the eighth three-match Test series without an individual hundred and just the second in England after the 1888 Ashes.Razaullah gives Pakistan something to cheerPakistan's biggest positive came from debutant Razaullah, who produced an exciting counter-attack at Edgbaston.His thrilling 81 off 63 balls gave Pakistan hope and briefly brought the third Test to life.But it was too late to change the outcome of the series.Pakistan have now lost 16 of their 21 Tests. Their difficult tour was followed by major changes, with seven players replaced in the squad after the second Test and coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul also removed.For England, the series marked a strong return after their disappointing results against New Zealand and the Ashes defeat.Root's return to the captaincy following Ben Stokes' retirement from international cricket also ended on a high.Marcus Trescothick, who took charge as interim red-ball head coach after Brendon McCullum's departure, will now hand over the side to Stephen Fleming ahead of England's three-Test tour of South Africa in December and January.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi in focus as India juggle opening dilemma and injury concerns against Afghanistan
articles.summary: Cricket News: New Delhi: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi was one of three squad members who attended the optional practice session ahead of the three-match T20I series against.
articles.body: New Delhi: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi was one of three squad members who attended the optional practice session ahead of the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan that begins on Sunday. Tilak Varma, who arrived earlier in the day, and Abhishek Sharma made up the trio who hit the nets at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi. Under the watchful eyes of India coach Gautam Gambhir, bowling coach Morne Morkel and batting coach Sitanshu Kotak, Sooryavanshi was the first to hit the nets and received regular feedback from Kotak, with conversation extending to almost 20 minutes in some instances.As the session progressed, the 15-year-old from Bihar was also involved in catching and fielding practices. A slight drizzle, however, interrupted the proceedings, forcing the groundstaff to bring out the covers. As the session drew to a close, Sooryavanshi once again had a long conversation with Gambhir and Kotak.The lengthy conversations appeared to suggest his involvement in the first contest of the series. Yet, the selectors will have a tough decision to make between his no-holds-barred approach versus Sanju Samson's equally aggressive batting, to open the batting alongside Abhishek Sharma."Having all three of them in the team is a luxury. They are flawless in their own departments. It is going to be a tight call because they have been performing consistently. Whoever gets the opportunity, it’s for the team’s benefit. For the players sitting outside, it’s important that I have an interaction with them along with the coach and give them that confidence that, no matter what, they will get their opportunity when the day comes," said Shreyas Iyer.Afghanistan skipper Ibrahim Zadran, who will step in as T20I skipper for the first time, acknowledged the prowess of Sooryavanshi. He admitted that they have made plans for the left-hander and the knowledge of his Orange Cap-winning show in the IPL has put him on the radar.It is going to be a tight call because they have been performing consistently. Whoever gets the opportunity, it is for the team's benefitSooryavanshi, who scored 776 runs in the IPL, didn't have a positive start to life on the international stage, mustering 14, 13 and 15 runs, respectively, in three T20Is against England before giving way to Samson in the dead rubber in Southampton. The returns turned fruitful in Zimbabwe, though, with series-topping 151 runs, including a smashing 18-ball 50 and a 49-ball 81.On Friday, as Indian team broke into spinners and seamers against the batters, Sooryavanshi struggled to cope with Jasprit Bumrah's sheer pace. As the ball seamed off the surface, the Samastipur-born was beaten multiple times and found it daunting to deal with the challenge that is Jasprit Bumrah.Alas, Afghanistan don't hold the bowling quality that Bumrah produces. Rather, most teams don't. Under Delhi's hot and humid conditions, with one eye skyward due to recent rains, Sooryavanshi could be persisted with alongside former top-ranked T20I batter Abhishek.Away from the top of the order dilemma, another point of worry for the Indian team will be the rising injury count ahead of the Asian Games in Japan. So much so that BCCI has begun hunting for a new Sports Science and Medicine head at the Centre of Excellence (CoE).Jasprit Bumrah, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Washington Sundar and Varun Chakaravarthy are all making their return to cricket after time away from the field.Iyer said the injury count is not frustrating while stressing that the sheer volume of cricket currently is bound to affect the players sooner rather than later."I feel it’s not frustrating. We need to understand, first of all, the amount of matches a player is playing continuously, rigorously. He’s bound to get injured some way or the other because the intensity is pretty high," said the India skipper on the eve of the T20I series."We also need to understand that not every player thinks of getting injured deliberately. It is because they are putting in efforts for the team, and if that effort turns out to be on the negative side, you can’t control it.""All you can control is whoever is available on that given day, and we need to give that sort of confidence to that particular player.""Talking about the combination, I feel that it certainly impacts the combination, but we know how all the players are. Even if there is a backup, he’s equally important for the team, and we know that they can deliver as well," he added.India squad: Sheryas Iyer (captain), Sanju Samson (wk), Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan (wk), Tilak Varma, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Shivam Dube, Washington Sundar, Axar Patel, Jasprit Bumrah, Arshdeep Singh, Vaibhav Sooryvanshi, Yash Thakur, Varun Chakravarthy, Ravi Bishnoi.Afghanistan squad: Ibrahim Zadran (captain), Darwish Rasooli, Noor ul Rahman, Rahmanullah Gurbaz (wk), Sediqullah Atal, Azmatullah Omarzai, Rashid Khan, Mohammed Nabi, Gulbadin Naib, Nangeliya Kharote, Abdollah Amhedzai, Fazalhaq Farooqi, Naveen-ul-Haq, Mujeeb ur Rahman, Noor Ahmed.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Pakistan cricket: New Zealander Mike Hesson interested in Test coach role and was approached by England
articles.summary: Mike Hesson is interested in coaching Pakistan's Test side on a permanent basis - and says he was approached earlier this year about the England job.
articles.body:
Mike Hesson is interested in coaching Pakistan's Test side on a permanent basis - and says he was approached about the England job earlier this year.

The 51-year-old New Zealander was drafted in by the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on an interim basis to replace Sarfaraz Ahmed for third Test at Edgbaston.

Sarfaraz was relieved of his duties after Pakistan suffered heavy defeats by England at Headingley and Lord's.

Hesson, who was appointed Pakistan's limited-overs coach in May 2025, oversaw an eight-wicket defeat by England in Birmingham but there were some encouraging signs.

"I'll be open to it, for sure. I love Test cricket," Hesson said.

"I think there's enough talent around the system in Pakistan that if we can provide some good direction, we can make some strides forward.

"It's certainly not going to happen in a game or two, but I think there is some skill there I'd certainly be considering looking after."

Hesson previously coached New Zealand between 2012 and 2018 and said he was approached by the England and Wales Cricket Board over replacing Brendon McCullum.

England sacked McCullum as their Test coach in July and subsequently named another Kiwi in Stephen Fleming as his successor.

"I was contacted by my agent to say there had been an approach to have a discussion around my availability, as I'm sure many people were," Hesson added.

"I made it pretty clear I had committed to Pakistan.

"Most of the positions I've been in, I've been in for five or six years. I see it through, then you have a break, then you refresh and try for something else."

Former Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja said Pakistan's players "put up a fight" in the eight-wicket defeat at Edgbaston but the red-ball side needs to receive more focus if they are to have any success.

"It's time to revisit Test match cricket," Ramiz told BBC Test Match Special.

"It's back to the drawing board because in the sub-continent not a lot of emphasis is put on Test match cricket.

"Obviously there was mayhem around the team and that may have hurt the dressing room environment. But Pakistan were also a little underdone, undercooked with preparation."

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Joe Root says Test side in better place than at the start of tumultuous summer
articles.summary: Captain Joe Root says England are in a better place at the end of their tumultuous summer and is impressed by how they have handled the chaos.
articles.body:
Captain Joe Root said England are in a better place at the end of their tumultuous summer than at the start after he helped seal a 3-0 series win over Pakistan.

Root hit 62 not out and Jordan Cox ended unbeaten on 59 as England survived a scare to beat Pakistan by eight wickets in the third Test at Edgbaston.

It provided a successful end to a summer that has included the shock retirement of captain Ben Stokes, the sacking of Test coach Brendon McCullum and various off-field issues.

"In chaos you learn a lot about the group of players you have," Root said.

"For us to have come through this series in the manner we have done, the way we've gone about our cricket, and gone about things has been really pleasing."

Root first regained the captaincy for the second Test against New Zealand in June after Stokes - who had been backed to remain in post alongside McCullum after last winter's Ashes defeat by Australia - was left out after breaking a team curfew.

After Stokes retired following the series defeat by New Zealand a Test later, McCullum was sacked and Root given the captaincy on a full-time basis for a second time.

Amid changes in personnel given the absence of Stokes, Root, who was Test captain from 2017 to 2022, has brought a calming presence to the role.

A side previously questioned for their professionalism has appeared more mature and adaptable, though the build-up to the second Test was overshadowed an incident involving bowler Brydon Carse outside a nightclub in Derby .

"There's been a lot of chaos around this series before a ball was bowled and the way we've handled it on and off the field, the way everyone understands what is expected of them - both as a player and how we want to carry ourselves - is a really good thing," Root said.

"The start of the series we wanted 3-0 and we've been clinical enough to do that."

Players such as Dan Lawrence, who came into the side in place of Stokes, and Cox have impressed, as had the four-man pace attack until struggles against the Pakistan lower order on Friday in Birmingham .

Root said he believed the team's development off the field is most significant.

"We're not the finished article," Root told BBC Test Match Special. "We're not going to kid ourselves. That'll be a constant work [in progress].

"The culture of this team is not something that's going to happen overnight, it's something we're going to have to live and breathe day in, day out.

"It's a good set of lads, really good guys that work incredibly hard and performances like this and commitment to what we're trying to achieve, both on and off the field, will be what earns trust and respect to everyone that supports us."

Former England captain Michael Vaughan agreed the team is a "work in progress".

"We can't judge this England team against Pakistan," he said.

"Let's not get too excited but what you see is a huge amount of talent.

"You have Jordan Cox looking so calm, England's greatest [Root] at number four, Harry Brook a generational talent, Dan Lawrence has fitted in lovely and Jamie Smith, whose keeping has been brilliant and batting has looked good.

"But they have not won a five-Test series since 2017. That is what you get judged on."

articles.title: 1980s AI photo trend: Jasprit Bumrah, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Shreyas Iyer get hilarious makeovers - WATCH
articles.summary: The portraits, featured in a video shared by the BCCI, showed the players in classic 1980s looks, complete with bell-bottom jeans, big sunglasses and retro h...
articles.body:
NEW DELHI: Social media has found a fun new way to bring the 1980s back, with AI turning modern-day pictures into vintage portraits. The trend has now reached the Indian cricket team, with several players enjoying a hilarious surprise ahead of their T20I series against Afghanistan in Delhi.

Two days before the series, the Indian players gathered at their hotel for a photo session. But before it began, they found a table filled with AI-generated pictures of themselves. The portraits, featured in a video shared by the BCCI, showed the players in classic 1980s looks, complete with bell-bottom jeans, big sunglasses and retro hairstyles. India allrounder Axar Patel and Abhishek Sharma picked up the portraits and burst out laughing as they showed them to their teammates. Jasprit Bumrah also joined in the fun. Sanju Samson, Washington Sundar, Shreyas Iyer, Tilak Varma and Shivam Dube checked out their retro pictures and appeared amused by their new 1980s avatars.

Ishan Kishan, who recently led East Zone to Duleep Trophy glory, fully embraced the retro look. He held up his AI-generated picture, sang and posed for the camera as his teammates enjoyed the moment. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Yash Thakur and Ravi Bishnoi also broke into smiles after seeing their 1980s avatars.

India and Afghanistan will face each other in a three-match T20I series, starting Sunday at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in Delhi. The second and third T20Is will be played on Tuesday and Thursday at the same venue.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Joe Root says England are 'well placed' for South Africa series as series victory ends chaotic Test summer
articles.summary: England captain Joe Root says his side are "well placed" ahead of South Africa Test series in December; His side secured 3-0 series whitewash of Pakistan with eight-wicket win at Edgbaston; watch England face Sri Lanka in a T20I live on Sky Sports at 6:30pm Tuesday
articles.body:
Root (62no) and No 3 batter Jordan Cox (59no) put on a 128-run partnership that led England to an eight-wicket victory in the third Test at Edgbaston, bringing a positive end to a tumultuous summer that has seen a change in head coach, a new captain and numerous off-field issues make headlines.

The captain lauded his team's professionalism and work ethic and praised their ability in the face of outside noise on the way to their comprehensive series win.

"I think we're in a better place than we were, definitely," Root said. "Just having gone through [a tumultuous summer], I think you learn in chaos.

"You learn a lot about the group of players that you have, and for us to have come through this series as we have done, the way that we've gone about our cricket has been really pleasing, and as I say, [we want to] be a continuation of that now.

"In terms of everything that we've been through over the the last little while, for us to now be able to have the clarity and come through the other side of chaos, I think is a a really important part.

"You can only deal with what's in front of you, right? And once once everything unfolded how it did, it was how we responded to that, and that was the most important thing. And I think the group have done that brilliantly.

Root: Pakistan pushback was good for the group

A satisfied Root reflected on what turned into a challenging third Test for England after a heroic 81 off 63 from Pakistan youngster Razaullah on day three left England with a target to chase, claiming that Pakistan's resurgence will benefit his side in the long term:

"The fact that we've been able to start that journey and win a series in the manner that we have done has been really pleasing.

"We've had things go our way throughout the series. We had a little bit of pushback yesterday [from Pakistan] which, in a strange way, was quite a good thing for the group.

"Fair play to Razaullah, he made things difficult for us. He played some wonderful shots and made it very difficult to set fields to. He struck the ball nicely - I don't know how he didn't pull a muscle, swinging the bat that hard.

"But for us to come through that and be so convincing in the way we've finished the series - throughout the whole three games - has been really pleasing.

"We were clinical towards the back end there, a big partnership to see us home. It's exactly the sort of thing we're after and puts us in a nice place going into the winter."

'Runs were hard to come by - not just for us'

Concerns have been raised over the century-making ability of Root's side, with both England and Pakistan failing to register a single ton despite making 17 half-centuries across the three-Test series, marking the first trilateral Test series in England without a hundred since the 1888 Ashes.

Root, though, brushed off worries over his side's run-making, and praised his side's performance in challenging batting conditions.

"I think everyone would want to go on [and make a century] after getting yourself in, but it has also been the nature of the summer and the surfaces we've had - it has been across the board, not just necessarily us.

"The pleasing thing is, from 2-2 [after the first over if the second innings], to be able to see that home with [Root and Cox] set at the end is a step forward in the right direction.

"It would almost be more concerning if we were relying on just one or two individuals who were scoring hundreds consistently. The fact that everyone is contributing shows that they're good enough to perform at this level.

"We'll have different challenges in the winter and different surfaces, but can we keep taking strides forward as a group... that being one of them, guys going on and making those big contributions.

"That being said, we still made 400 twice in these conditions."

First Test (Headingley) - England won by innings and 103 runs

Second Test (Lord's) - England won by 194 runs

Third Test (Edgbaston) - England won by eight wickets

articles.title: 'I definitely know how his mind works': Shreyas Iyer on Gautam Gambhir
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: India captain Shreyas Iyer believes his good understanding with head coach Gautam Gambhir can help India maintain clear communication and a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India captain Shreyas Iyer believes his good understanding with head coach Gautam Gambhir can help India maintain clear communication and an attacking mindset in T20 cricket. India will face Afghanistan in the first T20I at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi on Sunday.Iyer and Gambhir have worked together at Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR), where they helped the franchise win the IPL title in 2024. Iyer was the captain, while Gambhir was the mentor.Iyer believes Gambhir's aggressive approach and his ability to understand individual players can help the team stay clear about their roles."I feel that he has got a very aggressive mindset. He is someone who is always looking to win when he steps onto the field. He wants every individual to perform, which is pretty much given as a coach. So, he builds a lot of trust and confidence amongst the team, and every player knows what their role and clarity is."So, I think all these alignments are very much important when it comes to coaching skills, and he has got an amazing one-on-one player management approach. So, that is essential going forward in the tournament when you have that kind of relationship with every player because all of us are different in our own ways and you need to understand a certain player."Iyer understands Gambhir's approachIyer and Gambhir did not have an ideal start after India lost series in Ireland and England. Iyer then led India to a 3-0 series win over Zimbabwe in July, with VVS Laxman serving as the stand-in head coach.Having worked with Gambhir at KKR, Iyer said he already has a good idea of how the India coach thinks and approaches the game."Both of us, Gauti bhai and I, have been in this scenario where we need to know the players and how they can deliver for the team. The more matches we win, the more we would be getting to know each other closely. I have worked with him in the past in KKR. So, I definitely know how his mind works and how his approach is going to be," said Iyer in the pre-match press conference on Saturday.India focus on Afghanistan firstAfghanistan will be India's first challenge, with several of their players familiar with Indian conditions after playing in the IPL.Iyer said India would not look too far ahead and would instead focus on the opening game."See, we will go game by game. We don't have to think too much about the future. We are thinking about the first game. We know that Afghanistan is a nice team, and our preparation has also been promising for the last couple of days. Players are in great shape and mindset."So, we have to stay in the present and see to it that we deliver when the time comes. Leading up to the Asian Games, we have got a great opportunity to play against a very quality side. So, looking for a great competition and yes, fingers crossed. We will deliver to the best of our abilities."Iyer excited about first Asian GamesIyer is also looking forward to his first Asian Games, where he will lead India in their bid to defend the gold medal.The India captain said he is excited about meeting athletes from different sports and learning more about their mindset."It is definitely an exciting time for me and also for the team because it is going to be my first time, and there are a couple of players who have already been in the last Asian Games.“So, an exciting time. The first match we are going to play is against Japan. So, that is going to be a historic one, and I will be sharing a relationship with the hockey players and other Olympic players and athletes who will be there along with us."Definitely would be a great interaction, and I would be eagerly waiting to go there and interact with them and know what their mindset is. Probably go to one of the games and cheer for them as well. So, yes, we are going as a whole nation and then definitely we want to see to it that we come back triumphant," he concluded.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: England cricket: Why summer of 2026 has left Joe Root's side with more questions than answers
articles.summary: Are England a better team in September than in June? BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt discusses the positives and negatives of the Test summer and what the next period may bring.
articles.body:
It is 2026 and Joe Root is again England Test captain and Kevin Pietersen is back in the fold.

For those two things to be the new normal says plenty about the upheaval in one of the most turbulent summers in English cricket's recent history.

The debate as to whether there should have been alterations to the leadership after the Ashes has become a moot point, because England have nevertheless ended in a post-Bazball era.

Has the lack of change in the spring led to a wasted summer? Try telling any of Jordan Cox, Emilio Gay or Dan Lawrence that the summer has been wasted. Or a resurgent Ollie Robinson. Or Root, who had to rummage around his garage to dig out his old captain's blazer.

Are England a better team in September than they were in June? It is hard to argue that a team that has lost Ben Stokes has improved, though that should take nothing away from all the good things England have done in the 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan .

It is not a criticism of Stokes to say his personality dominated the England team he led. By the end of his reign, England were characterised by what Stokes said and did.

Naturally, England are different under Root, a different personality to Stokes.

Until the third evening of the third Test at Edgbaston, most of those differences seemed positive. There had been a calmness about England's demeanour, perhaps because they had not been tested to that point.

That calmness eroded with every swing of Razaullah's blade . Two hours of chaos frazzled England and exposed old doubts from Root's first spell as captain. The skipper himself felt it necessary to duck off the field. Stokes rarely lost control in such a fashion.

Even after such a bruising session, there were some small positives. Stand-in coach Marcus Trescothick was happy to admit his disappointment at what had transpired, a shift in tone from the Kool Aid messaging of the Bazball boys.

In reality, we are ending the summer with no clear knowledge of how good this England team is, following a pattern of years gone by: the drawn Ashes in 2023, a shock defeat by Sri Lanka at The Oval at the end of 2024 and the failure to win the final Test against India last year.

And that is the ultimate frustration of England's Test performances in the four-plus years that Rob Key has been director of cricket.

When the defining series have rolled around, England have not won them. In between those big challenges there have been more questions than answers. The brass ring always remains just out of reach, always searching for the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.

England in better place than start of summer - Root

Who has given selectors food for thought? England-Pakistan player ratings

TMS podcast: Cox and Root guide England to clean sweep

For now, England have a blossoming four-man pace quartet that has drawn comparisons with the famous Ashes winners of 2005.

Robinson has ruled England's summer, taking his 28 wickets at an average of 9.32; the sort of statistics in keeping with Test cricket from before World War I.

With Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson bringing the pace, England have a Swiss army knife of an attack, albeit lacking a left-armer.

Still, England are only one injury away from some inexperienced reserves. Sam Cook, Sonny Baker, Matthew Fisher and Henry Crocombe have four caps between them. Brydon Carse is available, though it remains to be seen if England will take him on tour while the Derby incident is still under investigation . Perhaps the in-form Olly Stone is due a recall.

The challenge for England is to find the right blend to suit the winter. The four seamers could operate in South Africa and the one-off pink-ball 150th anniversary Test in Melbourne, but the two matches in Bangladesh in February will demand a change in formation.

Despite the burning summer, spin has become a redundant weapon. The list of candidates to play in Bangladesh is long because there is no outstanding one among them.

Shoaib Bashir, Jack Leach, Dom Bess, Will Jacks, James Coles, Mason Crane, Liam Patterson-White, Calvin Harrison and Jack Carson may all think they have a shout of being on the plane.

The incumbent is Dan Lawrence, who has not had many opportunities to show the value of his part-time off-breaks.

Lawrence's bowling gives him an advantage when Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury, probably leaving a choice between Jordan Cox and Emilio Gay for the first Test in South Africa in December.

Both men have made three half-centuries in their first summers as Test batters. Cox is extremely highly rated by the England management, who must decide how much weight to put on Gay's skill as a specialist opener.

The top of the order has emerged as England's biggest batting concern. Ben Duckett made the only century of the summer, yet averages 23 since the beginning of the Ashes.

Gay's average in his six Tests is below 25 and his frustration at his second-innings dismissal against Pakistan came out with a swish of his bat towards the stumps. His running between the wickets is jittery and he is rarely placed in an important position in the field.

Of all the issues around the batting, England need Root to rediscover his best. The captain ends the summer without a hundred for the first time since 2019 and with his lowest average in a home season since the same year.

This time last year, it was full steam ahead in the pursuit of India great Sachin Tendulkar. Now, the 1,643 runs to catch the Little Master look a little further away. The smart money will be on Root to come out of his funk, rather than this being the start of a late-career decline.

Root will meet incoming coach Stephen Fleming in the coming days to plot the route forward.

Along with Key - the great survivor of England's chaotic summer - the trio will look for a way to win the marquee series, to claim the major prizes on offer in the months ahead: in South Africa this winter, the Ashes next summer, in India in early 2028.

And this is where England find themselves yet again, with judgement reserved until biggest challenges.

Still grasping for the brass ring, still chasing the pot of gold.

articles.title: 'I don't put any pressure on myself': Harmanpreet Kaur ahead of Asia Cup final against Sri Lanka
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: India captain Harmanpreet Kaur wants her team to keep things simple and trust their strengths when they face Sri Lanka in the Women's Asia .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India captain Harmanpreet Kaur wants her team to keep things simple and trust their strengths when they face Sri Lanka in the Women's Asia Cup final on Sunday. India and Sri Lanka have been the two best teams in the tournament and will now meet for the title. Harmanpreet believes there is very little between the two sides."Whenever you are playing a match which is so important to win the tournament, that day it is all about just playing on your strength and backing your strength," Harmanpreet said at the pre-final press conference."Rather than trying too many things and thinking of doing something extraordinary, it is all about sticking to your strength, backing yourself and trusting your gut feeling."Sri Lanka defeated India in the final of the previous edition two years ago. However, Harmanpreet does not see Sunday's game as a contest between a stronger and weaker team.‘It is all about playing good cricket’Sri Lanka produced a strong performance in the 2024 final. India scored 165, but Sri Lanka chased down the target with eight wickets in hand."Last time when we played against Sri Lanka, they came up with some really solid plans and solid performances. T20 is all about on a given day who is going to play the best cricket, they are going to win," she said."There is no doubt about any team being stronger or any team being lesser than anyone. It is all about playing good cricket on an important day."India happy with team effortHarmanpreet has been pleased with the way different players have stepped up at different stages of the tournament."Everyone in the team is very important and their contribution means a lot to us. It is good to see that whoever is getting the opportunity, they are coming up with some really solid performances," she said."Our batting unit came up in difficult situations and still managed to get runs on the board, while whenever we are bowling, our bowlers have come up with some really solid performances."Batters need to spend time at the creaseHarmanpreet admitted that batting on the Dubai surface has not been easy. She said India's batters will need to spend some time at the crease before going for big shots."This pitch is a little tough to bat on, but at the same time we just need to back ourselves, back our strength. We know we have such a good batting lineup," she said."Whoever is doing well on that day should take the responsibility and finish the game for the team."Settled batter must take responsibilityHarmanpreet also praised Sri Lanka's bowling attack and said their ability to execute their plans has made them effective on the Dubai surface."You have to really spend some time and then you can go for your shot. Whoever is settled, that person needs to take the responsibility and play till the end," she said.India will also have to deal with Sri Lankan opener Chamari Athapaththu, who can change a game quickly. Harmanpreet said India will look to dismiss her early but will not focus only on her."We definitely want to take her wicket as soon as possible because we know how dangerous she is when she is batting. We want to come up with some solid plans against her, not only against her, but all the batters," she said.Harmanpreet not worried about tossHarmanpreet said she does not want to put pressure on herself over the toss, as it is something a captain cannot control."I don't put any pressure on myself because toss is something which I feel is not in my control. We have been playing here for almost two weeks. We know the conditions, the pitch, and I think it is all about trusting your plans, trusting your gut feeling and backing them," she said.The India captain also wants her players to stay calm and avoid unnecessary mistakes in the final."We have seen whenever we are trying to do something special or something extraordinary, we have always made so many mistakes," she said."Tomorrow's match is all about trusting yourself and trying to make fewer mistakes on the field. The team which makes fewer mistakes in an important game has more chances to win."India hope for strong fan supportHarmanpreet is also hoping Indian fans turn up in large numbers and give the team an extra boost during the final."They have been our biggest strength whenever we are playing. They come and cheer for us. They play a big part in our lives," she said."When the stadium is packed, you feel more positive and you want to do more for your team. They mean a lot to us and hopefully they will come and cheer for the teams tomorrow."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ishan Kishan’s leadership, bonding and youthful fearlessness: How East Zone ended exile-like wait for Duleep Trophy triumph
articles.summary: Cricket News: KOLKATA: When Ratan Kumar looks back at East Zone’s Duleep Trophy triumph, he does not point first to tactics, star players or match-winning performan.
articles.body: KOLKATA: When Ratan Kumar looks back at East Zone’s Duleep Trophy triumph, he does not point first to tactics, star players or match-winning performances. Instead, the coach credits something less tangible but equally decisive: a dressing-room culture built on trust, freedom and camaraderie.The title ended East Zone’s nearly 14-year wait for the prestigious trophy, and according to Kumar, it was the team’s unity that formed the foundation of the successful campaign.“The biggest thing was managing a group of top athletes from different states. When players come after performing internationally and for their respective states, coaching is not about telling them too much. It is about giving them the right environment and preparation so that their desire to perform increases,” Kumar told STOI on Saturday.Having internationals such as Mohammed Shami, Mukesh Kumar and Ishan Kishan, alongside a host of young domestic cricketers, could easily have created divisions within the squad. Instead, Kumar said the group quickly developed a culture where every player felt comfortable expressing himself.“My first work, whether with Jharkhand or East Zone, is to create a culture where everyone can speak openly, where seniors and juniors share the same space, and where everyone feels valued,” he said.The coach revealed that the strong bonding within the squad became visible both on and off the field, with players from different states naturally mixing during the tournament.“You would see Jharkhand players sitting with Bengal players; Subhranshu Senapati, who is the Odisha captain (though he did not get a game), sitting with others and contributing to the team as part of the leadership group. It didn’t feel like they belonged to different teams. That atmosphere was very important. Teams win when they play cricket in a good environment.”A key figure in nurturing that atmosphere was skipper Ishan Kishan, whose leadership earned glowing praise from the coach.“Ishan’s understanding of the game is very deep. When you discuss something with him, you don’t need to think too much as a coach. He reads situations quickly, plans accordingly and communicates clearly with players,” Kumar said.While Kishan is often seen laughing and joking – and dancing, too, after the final – with teammates, Kumar said the wicketkeeper-batter possesses a sharp cricketing mind and an ability to stay composed in pressure situations.“He may look relaxed from the outside, but he has a very clear process. He responds to situations rather than reacting to them. He is an honest captain, his communication with players is excellent and that made my work much easier.”Kumar also singled out East Zone selectors and team management’s collective willingness to trust young players, a move that paid rich dividends. Players like Kumar Kushagra, Shikhar Mohan, Md Kounain Quraishi flourished after being given responsibility and freedom alongside senior pros like Anukul Roy and Virat Singh.While Jharkhand captain Singh made way for Mohan in the final, Quraishi came into the squad only after experienced Bengal spinning all-rounder Shahbaz Ahmad was left out with a niggle during their quarterfinal win against North East Zone.“What we wanted was that every youngster should get the opportunity to express himself. If someone got out after playing positively, nobody would make it a big issue. We wanted them to feel this was their stage,” says Kumar, who has once shared domestic dressing room with Mahendra Singh Dhoni.Among those youngsters, Kumar reserved special praise for Jharkhand’s emerging core, which increasingly shaped the team’s batting during the campaign.“Kushagra is a very elegant player. His technique is sound and he adapts well to every format. He is growing continuously and has the potential to play for India,” the former Bihar first-class cricketer said.The coach also highlighted the impact of teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, describing him as a rare cricketing talent whose fearlessness and understanding of the game stand out despite his age and someone who can change the dynamics of batting in red-ball cricket.For Kumar, East Zone’s title-winning run ultimately represented the perfect blend of experience and youth, guided by a captain who led from the front and sustained by a culture where every player felt empowered.“This championship had been awaited for a long time. We had a very good team this time, but more importantly, we had a very good atmosphere. I am grateful that I got the opportunity to coach such a group,” said Kumar.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Joe Root's best side in question ahead of South Africa tour and 2027 Ashes series
articles.summary: Sky Sports Cricket's pundits assess who stays and who goes with England's batting and bowling lineups yet to be decided ahead of a big 12 months; England tour South Africa before the 2027 Ashes; watch England vs Sri Lanka in a T20I on Tuesday live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
An eventful two months in English cricket has seen a the appointment of a new Test captain and head coach in Joe Root and Stephen Fleming amid a plethora of off-field issues that included multiple incidents involving alcohol and the retirement of previous captain Ben Stokes.

England's comprehensive series victory may have restored faith in a team who had previously lost seven of their last 10 Tests, but multiple questions relating to team personnel and leadership remain unanswered.

Here, the Sky Sports pundits assess the key dilemmas facing Root and Fleming...

Cox, Lawrence, Gay, Smith - who stays and who goes?

One of the most pressing issues facing England's selectors is that of the last remaining spot in an otherwise entrenched batting line-up.

Opener Emilio Gay, all-rounder Dan Lawrence, and wicketkeepers Jordan Cox and Jamie Smith have all featured in at least three of the summer's six Tests, but one of those four will have to drop out to facilitate the return of highly-rated Jacob Bethell, who has primarily featured as a No 3 for England.

Bethell has been tipped to open the batting in place of Gay - who has struggled after notching three half-centuries in six Tests this summer - while Cox has impressed both with the bat and in two days with the gloves after he replaced the injured Smith, notching a half-century in each of the three Tests against Pakistan.

"I would probably bring Bethell straight back in at three," Nasser Hussain said on the Sky Sports Cricket podcast. "You can't produce that hundred at Sydney the way he did and not have a Test match future.

"It's then Cox who looks vulnerable, or Gay - but I'm old school and think that opener is a specialist position.

"The two areas of English cricket we're looking for, a front-line spinner and opener.

"Gay has made a decent start, he looks like he could have a future but we're not certain. I would stick with him.

"The other option is you give Cox the gloves and axe Jamie Smith, but I also wouldn't do that. He's also done well with the gloves and got some runs."

England seamer Stuart Broad heaped on the praise for Jordan Cox after his composed 59no led England to victory in the third Test against Pakistan, adding: "I think Cox has done enough in this series to deserve a spot in the team.

"He's been composed, assured, calm, provided a match-winning innings today in a situation that was very difficult as a No 3 with England losing two wickets in the first over.

"That's the selector's biggest question - how do you get Cox in the team when Bethell is back.

"Huge credit to Cox for putting the selectors in that position - what I like about him is that he's got confidence in his own ability.

"One thing about this England team we've seen all summer is they lack a bit of leadership out on the field.

"I think Cox adds that. And I think he adds to the group and the leadership out there. I would have him in my XI come Pretoria in December."

The other area in discussion is that of England's bowling attack.

The four-pronged seam attack of Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue tore Pakistan's batting line-up to shreds for much of the series, restricting them to a score of under 200 in all of their first five innings and earning comparisons to the storied 2005 Ashes attack that interim head coach Marcus Trescothick called "fair" after the second Test.

Pakistan, though, were able to rebound on a flat Edgbaston pitch in their sixth innings, posting a score of 449 after a toiling day three performance that raised questions over whether England's bowlers were simply made to look good by favourable conditions.

Robinson in particular - who took a staggering 21 wickets at an average of 8.76 across the series - was questioned by Hussain, who identified his low speeds as a potential issue on more batter-friendly wickets.

"As we saw late yesterday - on England's one bad day - Robinson regressed to the mean, like the rest of the attack. His speeds were down and he was easier to play.

"He is what he is: he's a highly-skilled bowler, but if you keep him out there long enough, 78 mph becomes 74 mph - and that's a lot easier to face, even if it is nipping around a lot.

"You cannot argue though with his stats this summer. He's been absolutely fantastic with new-ball wickets up front. He sets the tone and wobbles it around - he's very difficult to play.

"Fleming, Root and whoever now just need to keep someone on his shoulder between now and South Africa, to make sure he rocks up fit for that first Test match."

Broad: We haven't learned a huge amount about Robinson

Broad, while complimentary of Robinson's success, feels the England seamer still has a lot to prove going into series against South Africa and Australia which will undoubtedly provide different challenges.

"Robinson looked relatively ineffective yesterday when it got a bit a bit flatter," Broad said on Sky Sports.

"Joe Root didn't trust him with the second new ball for more than two overs. But if he gets conditions where it nips around against this quality of batting unit, he's going to be highly effective.

"So I don't think we've learned a huge amount about Ollie Robinson. He's very good when conditions suit, but I expect the pitches to be different next summer.

"What I don't want to see is this trend of the keeper standing up to the stumps and the 75mph bowlers lobbing it up on a length continuing.

"At that level, you can have 25, 30 bowlers from county cricket that can do that job. On a normal Test match pitch, only five or six players can do that.

"Robinson has been given the ball in a summer that suited him, but there is no doubt that he delivered in an absolutely top-class way."

First Test (Headingley) - England won by innings and 103 runs

Second Test (Lord's) - England won by 194 runs

Third Test (Edgbaston) - England won by eight wickets
